images.caption:
View from front with the ablutions fountain before the mosque. 
The Belediye site (Google translated) has “Kurşunlu Complex is a work from the 16th century Ottoman period. It was built in 1517 by Çoban Mustafa Pasha, one of the viziers of the Ottoman Empire. According to the foundation record in the Topkapı Palace Museum Archive, all of the buildings in the complex, except the Great Caravanserai, were built by the vizier Çoban Mustafa Pasha between 1517 and 1525 and were probably completed in 1525. The architect of the Kurşunlu Complex is probably Acem Ali, who was the chief architect before Mimar Sinan. Acem Ali (also known as Acem Alisi or Esir Ali), whose real name is Alaeddin Ali Bey, was the first known chief architect in classical Ottoman architecture (1519-1537). The complex; It consists of a mosque, fountain, lodges (madrasa), training room, harem, imâret, mausoleum of Mevlevi sheikhs and two caravanserais.” The Turkish Wikipedia, though claiming the whole complex was by Sinan, adds a lodge part was at least for some time, till lodges were closed, used by a Mevlevi lodge. I earlier noted (source was lost) that only one caravanserai is listed as being by Sinan. I do not know what source to believe. 

Several parts of the complex are used for cultural purposes, like a meerschaum museum and short-term exhibitions.

images.caption: In part of the Kurşunlu Külliye is housed a museum showing the towns specialty, Lületaş, elsewhere known with the German word Meerschaum, a magnesium and silicon-based mineral, that is both lightweight and porous and moisture-absorbing. It seems to be ideal for the making of pipes, but can be worked into all sorts of objects. The region some 30 km southeast of Eskişehir has the largest deposits of meerschaum in the world.

images.caption: From a first visit I have always admired the town for seemingly considering its “old” houses not as “things of the past” but “things to be kept for the future”. During later visits many had not been torn down, but restored, in particular in an area called Odunpazarı (“Firewood market”). In 2018 I walked that specific region, paying attention to the old houses, many now splendidly restored, but also to the renovation works themselves and the contrasting “modern” buildings present also. In addition I visited some local artisans and took pictures of things that struck my fancy.
